overview.title: Introducing class activation heatmaps and Grad-CAM
overview.main_topic: The page ends the filter-visualization discussion (higher-layer filters look like feathers, eyes, leaves) and opens section 10.3: class activation map (CAM) visualization, the Grad-CAM method of Selvaraju et al., and Listing 10.17, which downloads and loads the elephant test image as a batched NumPy array.
overview.central_idea: A class activation heatmap scores every location of an input image by how important it is for a chosen class. Grad-CAM computes it by taking a conv layer's output feature map and weighting each channel by the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel, which turns 'how strongly each channel fires where' into 'how strongly the class is activated where'.
overview.importance: Grad-CAM is one of the most widely used interpretability tools for ConvNets. It answers the question users actually ask: why did the model predict this class, and where in the image is the evidence? It also reuses this chapter's ingredients: feature-map access and backend-specific gradients.
learning_objectives: Complete the filter hierarchy: what higher-layer filters resemble.
Explain what a class activation heatmap is and what it is used for (debugging, interpretability, localization).
Describe the Grad-CAM recipe in words and as a formula: channel weights from gradients, weighted sum of channel maps.
Explain the intuition 'activation intensity × channel importance = class activation intensity'.
Explain each line of Listing 10.17 and the shape of img_array.
prerequisites: Feature maps and channels of a conv layer (chapter 8)
Gradients of an output with respect to intermediate tensors (p.318-319)
Pretrained ImageNet classifiers such as Xception

summary:
The page opens with the **last bullet** of the filter hierarchy from p.322: filters in higher layers begin to resemble **textures found in natural images: feathers, eyes, leaves**, and so on.

**Section 10.3** then introduces a final visualization technique for understanding **which parts of an image led a ConvNet to its classification decision**. It is useful for "debugging" the decision process, especially when the model makes a mistake (the field of **model interpretability**), and it can also **locate specific objects** in an image.

The general family is **class activation map (CAM) visualization**: producing heatmaps of class activation over input images. A **class activation heatmap** is a 2-D grid of scores for one output class, computed for every location of the input, that indicates how important each location is for that class. In a dogs-versus-cats ConvNet you could produce a "cat" heatmap (how cat-like each part of the image is) and a separate "dog" heatmap.

The authors use **Grad-CAM** (Selvaraju et al., footnote 1, arXiv 1610.02391). It takes the **output feature map of a convolution layer** for a given input and **weights every channel by the gradient of the class with respect to that channel**. Intuitively, a spatial map of "how intensely the input activates different channels" is weighted by "how important each channel is with regard to the class", which gives a spatial map of "how intensely the input image activates the class".

The demonstration uses the pretrained **Xception** model on a photo of **two African elephants** (possibly a mother and calf) in the savanna (figure 10.7, next page). **Listing 10.17** downloads the image with `keras.utils.get_file` (cached locally under `img_path`), loads it as a PIL image with `keras.utils.load_img`, and converts it to a NumPy array with a batch dimension using `np.expand_dims(img, axis=0)`. Despite the listing's title, no model-specific scaling is applied yet. The next page uses a KerasHub classification task, which includes its own preprocessing.

paragraphs.excerpt: The filters in higher layers begin to resemble textures found in natural images:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Filters in higher layers begin to resemble textures from natural images, such as feathers, eyes and leaves.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This completes the three-level hierarchy started on p.322 (edges and colors, then simple textures, then natural-image textures). The block8 row of figure 10.6 shows curved strokes, eye-like spots and leaf-like shapes. These units have large receptive fields and combine many mid-level textures, so their preferred stimuli look like recognizable parts of objects, though still tiled as textures.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that deep units encode semantically meaningful parts, which is the kind of evidence a classifier needs. It is also why the last conv layer is the right place for Grad-CAM to look.

terminology.meaning: Layers close to the output of the convolutional base, e.g. block8 and above in Xception.

paragraphs.excerpt: Here’s one last visualization technique—one that is useful for understanding which parts of a
paragraphs.what_it_says: One last technique shows which parts of an image led the ConvNet to its classification decision. It helps debug the decision process, especially for misclassifications (model interpretability), and can also locate objects in an image.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Unlike the filter visualizations, which are about the model in general, this technique explains a specific prediction on a specific image. It gives a spatial attribution: which pixels or regions mattered for the predicted class. If a model calls an image 'wolf' because of snow in the background, the heatmap would light up on the snow, revealing a shortcut. Because the heatmap peaks where the evidence for a class is, it also acts as weakly supervised object localization, with no bounding-box labels needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Interpretability is crucial for trusting, debugging and improving models, and for spotting spurious correlations or dataset bias.

terminology.meaning: The study of explaining why a model produces its outputs, in terms humans can inspect.
Finding where in an image an object is.

paragraphs.excerpt: This general category of techniques is called class activation map (CAM) visualization, and it
paragraphs.what_it_says: These techniques are called class activation map (CAM) visualization: they produce heatmaps of class activation over input images. A class activation heatmap is a 2-D grid of scores for one output class, computed for every location of the input, indicating how important each location is for that class. For a dogs-versus-cats ConvNet you would get a 'cat' heatmap and a 'dog' heatmap. The implementation used is that of Selvaraju et al.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The heatmap is class-specific: the same image yields different maps for different classes. Its resolution is that of the chosen conv layer's spatial grid (coarse, e.g. a few cells per side for a last conv layer), and it is later upsampled onto the image for display. Each cell answers: how much does this region support class c?
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Class specificity is what makes CAM useful for explanation: you can ask 'where is the cat?' and 'where is the dog?' separately and see whether the model looks at the right regions.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the original CAM (Zhou et al., 2016) required a global-average-pooling architecture; Grad-CAM generalizes it to any ConvNet by using gradients.

terminology.meaning: A spatial map of how much each location of the input contributes to a particular class score.
Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Selvaraju et al.), the method used here.

connections: p.324: the Xception classifier used to produce the class scores

paragraphs.excerpt: Grad-CAM consists of taking the output feature map of a convolution layer, given an
paragraphs.what_it_says: Grad-CAM takes the output feature map of a convolution layer for a given input and weights every channel in it by the gradient of the class with respect to that channel. Intuitively, a spatial map of how intensely the input activates each channel is weighted by how important each channel is for the class, giving a spatial map of how intensely the input activates the class.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The feature map A has shape (H, W, K). Channel k is a spatial map A^k saying where feature k fires. The gradient of the class score y^c with respect to A^k says how much y^c would increase if channel k fired more, i.e. how important feature k is for class c. Combining the two (weight each channel, then aggregate over channels) gives an H×W map that is high where class-relevant features are active. The later code (p.325-328) reduces each channel's gradient to one number by averaging over space ('pooled_grads'), multiplies the channels by these weights, averages across channels, and keeps only positive values.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the whole algorithm in two sentences. The rest of section 10.3 is implementation: obtaining the gradient with each backend, then pooling, weighting and displaying.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The weight of channel k is alpha_k = mean over (i, j) of d y^c / d A^k_ij, and the heatmap is ReLU(sum_k alpha_k A^k). The book's code uses a mean over channels instead of a sum, which only rescales the map.

terminology.meaning: The (height, width, channels) output tensor of a conv layer.
How sensitive the class score is to a channel's activation, measured by the gradient.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The technique is demonstrated with the pretrained Xception model on an image of two African elephants, possibly a mother and her calf, walking in the savanna (figure 10.7). The first step is downloading the image and converting it to a NumPy array.

paragraphs.why_it_matters: A concrete, well-classified example makes it easy to judge whether the heatmap is sensible.

concepts.name: Class activation map (CAM)
concepts.definition: A 2-D grid of scores for a specific output class, one per location of the input image, indicating how important each location is for that class.
concepts.intuition: A 'where is the evidence for class c?' overlay on the image.
concepts.technical: Computed on a conv layer's spatial grid (coarse), then upsampled and overlaid on the input for display.
concepts.significance: Used to debug classifier decisions, detect spurious cues, and localize objects without box labels.
concepts.example: For a dogs-versus-cats ConvNet: a 'cat' heatmap and a 'dog' heatmap of the same photo.
concepts.misconception: A CAM is not a segmentation mask; it is coarse and shows relative importance, not exact object boundaries.

concepts.name: Grad-CAM
concepts.definition: Gradient-weighted class activation mapping: weighting each channel of a conv layer's output feature map by the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel, then aggregating into a heatmap.
concepts.intuition: Where features fire × how much the class cares about those features = where the class is activated.
concepts.technical: alpha_k^c = (1/Z) sum_{i,j} d y^c / d A^k_{ij}; L^c = ReLU(sum_k alpha_k^c A^k). The book's code (p.325-328) uses the last conv layer block14_sepconv2_act of Xception.
concepts.significance: Applicable to any ConvNet without retraining; it is one of the most widely used vision interpretability methods.
concepts.example: Heatmap for 'African elephant' on figure 10.7, expected to highlight the elephants.
concepts.misconception: Grad-CAM does not use the gradient with respect to the input pixels (that would be a saliency map); it uses the gradient with respect to a conv layer's feature map.

concepts.name: Model interpretability
concepts.definition: Understanding and explaining why a model makes the predictions it makes.
concepts.intuition: Opening the black box enough to see what it is looking at.
concepts.technical: This chapter covers four tools: intermediate activations, filter visualizations, class activation heatmaps and latent-space visualization.
concepts.significance: Essential for debugging misclassifications and building trust.
concepts.example: Checking whether a misclassified image's heatmap focuses on the background instead of the object.
concepts.misconception: A plausible-looking heatmap does not prove the model is reasoning correctly; it is one piece of evidence.

concepts.name: Hierarchy of learned features
concepts.definition: Edges and colors in low layers, textures in middle layers, natural-image textures (feathers, eyes, leaves) in higher layers.
concepts.intuition: Simple parts combine into complex parts.
concepts.technical: Completed on this page by the third bullet.
concepts.significance: It explains why the last conv layer is a good place for Grad-CAM: its features are the most class-relevant while still having spatial layout.
concepts.misconception: Higher layers do not lose all spatial information; they keep a coarse spatial grid, which is what Grad-CAM exploits.

math.title: Grad-CAM heatmap (formalizing the verbal description)
math.source_text: weighting every channel in that feature map by the gradient of the class with respect to the channel

variables.meaning: Activation of channel k at location (i, j) of the chosen conv layer's output feature map (shape H×W×K).
Score for class c (the top predicted class in the book's code).
Importance of channel k for class c: the spatially averaged gradient.
Class activation heatmap value at (i, j).
Spatial size and number of channels of the feature map.

math.operations: Take the gradient of the class score with respect to the feature map, average it over space to get one weight per channel, form the weighted combination of channel maps, and keep the positive part.
math.purpose: To turn channel activations into a single class-specific spatial map.
math.interpretation: Large positive L^c_{ij} means location (i, j) strongly activates features that increase the class score. The book's code (p.325-328) computes the channel-wise mean instead of the sum, which only scales the map, and then clips negatives with np.maximum(heatmap, 0).
math.intuition: 'How intensely the input activates each channel' × 'how important each channel is to the class' = 'how intensely the input activates the class' (book's wording).
math.numerical_example: Two channels on a 2×2 grid: $A^1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $A^2 = \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, with weights $\alpha_1 = 0.5$ and $\alpha_2 = -0.25$. The weighted sum is $\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0&-0.5\end{pmatrix}$, and the ReLU gives $\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so only the top-left cell supports the class.

code.title: Preprocessing an input image for Xception
code.original_code:
img_path = keras.utils.get_file(
    fname="elephant.jpg",
    origin="https://img-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/elephant.jpg",
)
img = keras.utils.load_img(img_path)
img_array = np.expand_dims(img, axis=0)
code.what_it_does: Downloads the elephant test image (once, then cached), loads it as a PIL image, and converts it to a NumPy array with a leading batch axis, ready to be fed to a model.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: 'Downloads the image and stores it locally under the path img_path.' get_file caches into the Keras data directory and returns the local path; later calls reuse the cached copy.
Callout: 'Returns a Python Imaging Library (PIL) image.' No target_size is given, so the image keeps its original resolution.
Callout: 'Converts to NumPy and adds a batch dimension.' np.expand_dims converts the PIL image to an array of shape (height, width, 3) and inserts a new axis 0, giving (1, height, width, 3).

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a URL. Output: img_array of shape (1, H, W, 3) with uint8 values in [0, 255] (H and W are the photo's own dimensions).
code.algorithm: Download, cache, decode, add batch axis.
code.theory_link: Keras models take batches, so a single image must become a batch of size 1.

parameters.name: fname
parameters.role: Local file name for the cached download.

parameters.name: axis=0
parameters.role: Position of the inserted batch axis.

pitfalls: Despite the listing title, no Xception-specific rescaling is done here. Inference: the KerasHub classifier task introduced on p.324 bundles its own preprocessing.
Forgetting the batch axis gives a shape (H, W, 3) input, which a model expecting (batch, H, W, 3) misreads or rejects.
np is NumPy and must already be imported (import numpy as np).

deeper.title: Grad-CAM step by step (preview of p.325-328)
deeper.body:
1. Choose a convolution layer, typically the **last** one, because it has the most class-relevant features but still a spatial grid. The book uses `block14_sepconv2_act` of Xception.
2. Run the image through the network up to that layer to get $A$ (shape $H\times W\times K$).
3. Run the rest of the network from $A$ to the class scores and pick the score $y^c$ of the target (top) class.
4. Compute $\partial y^c/\partial A$, which requires backend gradient APIs, as in section 10.2.
5. Average the gradient over space to get one weight per channel.
6. Multiply each channel of $A$ by its weight, average over channels, clip negatives, normalize, and overlay on the image.

The detailed steps are AI-written previews based on the code fragments in later pages; the core description (weight channels by gradients) is the book's.

deeper.title: Analogy: a committee of detectors
deeper.body: Imagine K specialists scanning the photo, each marking where they see their feature ('wrinkly skin', 'large ear', 'grass'). The class 'African elephant' trusts some specialists a lot (large positive gradient) and others not at all, or even negatively. Grad-CAM weights each specialist's marked-up map by how much the elephant decision trusts them, then stacks the maps. Where the trusted specialists agree, the heatmap glows.

deeper.title: Grad-CAM versus filter visualization
deeper.body:
| | Filter visualization (10.2) | Grad-CAM (10.3) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | What does filter k detect in general? | Where in *this* image is the evidence for class c? |
| Optimized/differentiated w.r.t. | Input pixels (gradient ascent) | Last conv feature map (one gradient, no optimization) |
| Output | Synthetic texture image | Coarse heatmap over a real image |
| Uses classifier head? | No (backbone only) | Yes (needs class scores, p.324) |

misconceptions.claim: Grad-CAM shows what a filter detects in general.
misconceptions.correction: That is filter visualization (10.2). Grad-CAM explains a specific prediction on a specific image, for a specific class.

misconceptions.claim: A class activation heatmap is the same for all classes.
misconceptions.correction: It is class-specific: the same image gives different 'cat' and 'dog' heatmaps (book's example).

misconceptions.claim: Grad-CAM uses the gradient with respect to the input pixels.
misconceptions.correction: It uses the gradient of the class score with respect to the channels of a conv layer's output feature map.

takeaways: Higher-layer filters resemble natural-image textures: feathers, eyes, leaves.
Class activation heatmaps show which parts of an image led a ConvNet to its decision; they are used for debugging (interpretability) and localization.
A CAM is a class-specific 2-D grid of importance scores over the input locations.
Grad-CAM weights each channel of a conv layer's output by the gradient of the class with respect to that channel: activation intensity × channel importance = class activation intensity.
Listing 10.17 downloads elephant.jpg, loads it as a PIL image and makes a (1, H, W, 3) NumPy batch.

questions.question: In Grad-CAM, each channel of the conv feature map is weighted by…
options: the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel
the gradient of the class score with respect to the input pixels
the channel's average activation over the dataset
a random weight learned during training
questions.answer: the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel
questions.explanation: The page defines Grad-CAM this way. Gradients with respect to pixels give a saliency map, not Grad-CAM. Dataset averages and random weights play no role.

questions.question: What is a class activation heatmap, according to the book?
questions.answer: A 2-D grid of scores associated with a specific output class, computed for every location in an input image, indicating how important each location is with respect to that class.

questions.question: A feature map has two channels on a 1×2 grid: A¹ = [2, 0], A² = [0, 3]. The channel weights are α₁ = 0.5 and α₂ = −1. Compute the Grad-CAM map ReLU(α₁A¹ + α₂A²).
questions.explanation: Only the first location supports the class; the negative contribution at the second location is clipped, as in np.maximum(heatmap, 0) later in the section.

questions.question: What is the shape of img_array in Listing 10.17, and why is the extra axis needed?
questions.answer: (1, height, width, 3). The leading axis is a batch dimension, because Keras models process batches of inputs.
questions.explanation: The callout says np.expand_dims 'converts to NumPy and adds a batch dimension'.

questions.question: Give two uses of class activation heatmaps mentioned on the page.
questions.answer: Debugging the decision process of a ConvNet, especially for classification mistakes (model interpretability), and locating specific objects in an image.
questions.explanation: Both appear in the first paragraph of section 10.3.

questions.question: Explain in your own words the intuition for why multiplying channel activations by channel gradients yields a class heatmap.
questions.answer: The activations say where each feature is present; the gradients say how much each feature matters for the class. Their product, combined across channels, is high where class-relevant features are present, i.e. where the image 'activates the class'.
questions.explanation: The book phrases it as weighting 'how intensely the input image activates different channels' by 'how important each channel is with regard to the class'.

questions.question: What do filters in higher layers begin to resemble, according to the bullet that opens the page?
options: Textures found in natural images, such as feathers, eyes and leaves
questions.answer: Textures found in natural images, such as feathers, eyes and leaves
questions.explanation: Edges and colors describe the first layers (p.322), uniform patches are not the book's description of higher layers, and heatmaps are a different technique.

questions.question: Can you explain the difference between filter visualization and Grad-CAM in two sentences, including what each differentiates with respect to?
questions.answer: Filter visualization runs gradient ascent on the input pixels to show what a filter detects in general. Grad-CAM takes the gradient of a class score with respect to a conv feature map to show where in a particular image the evidence for that class lies.
